sentences.text: Some octopuses can change color so fast, it looks like a special effect. But there's no paint, and no invisibility switch.
One key part of the trick is thousands of structures called chromatophores. Each contains a stretchy sac filled with pigment.
Nerves control tiny muscles around each sac. When those muscles contract, they pull the sac open, making its color more visible.
When the muscles relax, the sac shrinks, and that pigment becomes less visible again.
Changing the pattern across the skin helps the animal blend into its surroundings, hiding from predators or approaching prey.
It can change texture too. Skin projections called papillae can make the surface bumpy or spiky, helping match rocks and coral.
So, who needs an invisibility cloak when your skin already has a special-effects department?
